stem:
Blood entering a pulmonary capillary of a healthy 40-year-old man has a partial pressure of oxygen of 40 mm Hg, while the adjacent alveolar air has a partial pressure of oxygen of 104 mm Hg.

Which of the following best describes the resulting movement of oxygen across the respiratory membrane in this region?

options.label: A
options.text: Diffusion from the capillary blood into the alveolus
options.misconception: The direction of the partial-pressure gradient is being reversed.
options.explanation: Gases move from higher to lower partial pressure; alveolar pressure (104) exceeds blood pressure (40), so oxygen moves into the blood, not out of it.

options.label: B
options.text: Rapid diffusion from the alveolus into the capillary blood
options.misconception: None; oxygen moves down its partial-pressure gradient into the blood.
options.explanation: The roughly 64 mm Hg difference creates a very strong pressure gradient that causes oxygen to rapidly cross the respiratory membrane from the alveoli into the blood.

options.label: C
options.text: Active transport of oxygen into the capillary blood
options.misconception: An energy-requiring carrier process is being proposed for oxygen uptake.
options.explanation: Oxygen crosses the respiratory membrane by simple diffusion down its partial-pressure gradient; no active transport is involved.

options.label: D
options.text: Facilitated diffusion of oxygen through membrane carrier proteins
options.misconception: A carrier-mediated mechanism is being assigned to a directly permeable gas.
options.explanation: Oxygen diffuses directly through the membrane lipids without carriers; the rate is set by the partial-pressure gradient.

options.label: E
options.text: No net movement, because the two compartments have equilibrated
options.misconception: A 64 mm Hg difference is being mistaken for equilibrium.
options.explanation: Equilibrium requires equal partial pressures; the large alveolar-to-blood difference drives continuous diffusion.

context: Learning objective: predict gas movement from partial pressures. A roughly 64 mm Hg alveolar-to-blood PO2 gradient drives rapid oxygen diffusion across the respiratory membrane.
